note: A closed /# … #/ comment is removed before parsing; the spaces around it are the author's and both remain.
Strip runs before the cosmetic stage: the double space the comment leaves is then collapsed and the first letter capitalized.

An unterminated /# is NOT a comment — the reference regex /\/#[\s\S]*?#\//g needs the closer, so the text stays. A port that drops from /# to end of input removed whole documents (spintax-win, fixed 2026-08-06).
The everyday shape of the unterminated-opener rule: a URL fragment starts with /# and must survive when no #/ follows anywhere.

NEGATIVE guard for the case above: matching is lazy from the FIRST /# to the FIRST #/, so once a real closer exists later, the opener inside the URL starts the comment and the fragment is consumed with it. Sharp, but it is the family rule — widening it (e.g. smarter opener detection) is a contract change.
Lazy matching ends each comment at the nearest closer, so two comments strip separately instead of one span swallowing the text between them.
Comments do not nest: the first closer ends the comment, the inner /# is swallowed as comment text, and the now-unpaired trailing #/ is ordinary text.
A comment may span lines; its inner newlines vanish with it, while the author's newlines around it remain.
A #set inside a comment is stripped before directive extraction: the definition never exists and the reference stays an undefined %x% rendered literally.

Verdict half of the unterminated-opener rule: /# without a closer strips NOTHING, so the brace after it is still there to diagnose. An engine that swallows to end of input calls this valid and loses the diagnostic with the text.
The mirror case: a CLOSED comment removes its content before validation, so broken markup inside it is invisible and the template is valid.
An unterminated /# is ordinary text, not a syntax error of its own.
extract() sees the comment-stripped text: a #set, an #include and a %ref% inside a closed comment contribute nothing; the live ones outside are collected.
A /! … !/ span is emitted exactly as written: braces, brackets, a reference and a hash inside are text (#92, ADR 0001). Guards an engine without the construct, which spins the content.
One scanner for both block constructs: inside a span, /# and #/ are content and come back (ADR 0001 rule 1). Guards an engine that strips comments before it looks for spans.
Negative of the case above: whichever opener comes first wins, so a /! inside a comment is removed with it and the !/ after the comment is plain text.
The span opens first, so the /# inside it is content and the #/ after it is plain text. Guards an engine that runs the comment pass first (it would remove "/# b !/ c #/").

An opener with no closer is two characters of text and the scan goes on after it — the reading of the alternation /\/#[\s\S]*?#\/|\/![\s\S]*?!\//g. So a comment after an unclosed /! is still removed. Guards a scanner that stops at the first unclosed opener (stripComments did, which was equivalent while there was one construct).
The same rule the other way: a span after an unclosed /# is still a span.
The closer is searched from the END of the opener, so /!/ does not close itself: /!/x!/ is the span "/x". Guards an engine that searches from the opener's slash.
Negative of the case above: a /!/ with no later !/ is plain text.
An empty span /!!/ is removed, like an empty comment, and leaves nothing behind.
Because an empty span leaves no token, the first letter after it is still the first letter of the text. Guards an engine that keeps an empty token in place.
Two spans that touch are two spans: the first closer ends the first one.
Spans do not nest: the first !/ closes, the inner /! is content and the trailing !/ is plain text.
Negative guard: a !/ with no opener before it is plain text and the markup around it renders as usual.
